prompt.context: Our client is a manufacturer and dealer of heavy industrial trucks. They currently offer three brands of trucks. Each brand offers trucks in the light-, mid- and heavy-duty class. The client currently sells trucks directly to end users and typically includes a clause to repurchase the trucks after a few years.
prompt.question: What are some areas our client should be concerned about?

clarifying_info.q: How many players are in the market?
clarifying_info.a: The market is composed of three players (companies, not brands).

clarifying_info.q: What is the relative market share among players?
clarifying_info.a: Players are fairly equal in market share.

clarifying_info.q: Are the client's three brands differentiated from one another?
clarifying_info.a: The client's brands are not distinguished and are direct competitors with one another.

exhibits.title: Repurchase Agreement
exhibits.shows: Terms of the client's repurchase agreement with end users, showing length of service, repurchase price, the number of trucks to be repurchased each year, and the resale price the client can achieve for repurchased trucks each year.

exhibits.title: In-house vs. Procured Parts
exhibits.shows: Two tables comparing the client and two competitors: (1) the percentage of parts that are in-house vs. purchased, and (2) the relative cost per part for in-house vs. purchased parts (client in-house = 100% index).

framework: Repurchase agreement liability — size the financial exposure from buying back trucks at a fixed price when resale values are declining
Brand proliferation — evaluate whether maintaining three competing in-house brands is optimal or whether streamlining creates value
Part procurement strategy — compare in-house vs. purchased part cost structures against competitors to find cost reduction levers
Market structure — consider competitive dynamics given equal three-player market share and lack of brand differentiation

questions.prompt: Size the total liability created by the repurchase agreement over its three-year life.
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize that the client repurchases trucks at $25,000 but can only resell them at below that price, creating a loss per truck. Losses grow each year as resale value declines and volume increases. Strong candidates flag this as the most important concern identified in brainstorming.

math.setup: Loss per truck = Repurchase price ($25,000) minus Resale price each year. Total liability = trucks repurchased each year × loss per truck, summed over 3 years.

questions.prompt: What strategies could reduce the repurchase liability, and what are the trade-offs?
questions.guidance: Candidate should propose: (1) Accelerate repurchases — buy back trucks earlier when the loss per truck is smaller; however, more used trucks on the market could cannibalize new truck sales. (2) Increase resale price through refurbishment — only viable if the net margin on refurbishment is positive. Candidate should quantify the savings from accelerating repurchases if asked.

math.setup: Assume 50% of Year 2 and Year 3 trucks are repurchased one year earlier (i.e., in Year 1 and Year 2 respectively), reducing the loss per truck by $2,000 for those trucks.
steps: Savings: 35,000 trucks × $2,000 loss reduction/truck = $70M liability reduction
math.answer: Accelerating 50% of Year 2 and Year 3 repurchases saves approximately $70M in liability. Other feasible acceleration plans are acceptable.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, calculate the client's current absolute cost of in-house and procured parts, then assess the opportunity if the client could match the best-in-class cost structure for each category.
questions.guidance: Candidate should use total truck cost ($40,000) and part mix percentages to derive absolute costs. Then apply the relative cost indices to identify the price leader for each category (Competitor A for in-house at 80%; Competitor B for purchased at 80%) and calculate savings. Strong candidates also hypothesize why competitors have better cost structures (economies of scale, vertical integration) and note feasibility constraints.

math.setup: Total truck cost = $40,000. In-house share = 40%; Purchased share = 60%. Relative cost index: client in-house = 100% baseline. Best in-house = Competitor A at 80% of client. Best purchased = Competitor B at 80% of client's purchased cost (client is at 120% vs. Competitor B at 80%, so client pays 120/80 = 1.5× more, meaning a 1/3 or ~33% reduction).
steps: Total savings: $3,200 + $8,000 = $11,200 per truck (≈ 28% of total truck cost)
math.answer: Client could save approximately $11,200 per truck (28%) if it matched best-in-class cost structure in both categories. This is a significant opportunity but feasibility must be assessed.

brainstorming.prompt: What are some areas our client should be concerned about?

categories.name: Repurchase Agreement
ideas: Fixed repurchase price creates liability when resale values decline
Growing volume of repurchases amplifies the liability over time
Used truck inventory competes with new truck sales

categories.name: Brand Proliferation
ideas: Three competing in-house brands erode each other's sales without differentiation
Opportunity to streamline to one brand to reduce complexity and improve scale
Shared parts and platforms across brands could reduce costs

categories.name: Part Procurement
ideas: In-house production may lack scale efficiency versus best-in-class competitors
Procured parts cost more relative to at least one competitor
Opportunity to adjust make-vs.-buy decisions or acquire a supplier

categories.name: Market & Competitive Dynamics
ideas: Equal three-player market share means limited pricing power
Lack of brand differentiation limits premium pricing
Market share shifts could alter repurchase volumes significantly

recommendation: Client should accelerate repurchases where possible to reduce the $310M liability, recognizing the largest exposure is in Years 2 and 3
Client should investigate changing its part procurement strategy — matching best-in-class in-house and purchased costs could reduce truck cost by up to $11,200 (28%)
risks: Accelerating repurchases floods the market with used trucks, potentially cannibalizing new truck sales
Reducing new truck costs (without capturing the margin) makes used trucks less appealing and could increase repurchase liability by reducing resale values
These two strategies can negatively interact: improvements in one area may worsen the other
next_steps: Better understand market elasticity for used and new trucks to quantify cannibalization risk before committing to an acceleration strategy
Conduct a detailed make-vs.-buy analysis and assess feasibility of matching competitor cost structures or acquiring a parts supplier
Evaluate whether consolidating from three brands to one improves scale economics and reduces internal competition
